title: Duplex
full_review:
����������� A young New York couple's dream apartment turns into a domestic nightmare when they find out that it comes equipped with a high-maintenance, elderly tenant in the dark screwball comedy "Duplex" (Miramax).

Though frequently funny, the film, directed by Danny DeVito (who lends his voice to narration but does not appear in the movie) subscribes to a problematic brand of pitch-black humor that tickles viewers' funny bones with a feather of murderous cruelty.

For Alex (Ben Stiller), an aspiring novelist, and Nancy (Drew Barrymore), a hotshot magazine layout designer, the future couldn't be brighter. The only piece missing from their American dream puzzle is a home of their own. This speed bump on the yellow brick road to yuppie nirvana is remedied when their shady real-estate agent (Harvey Fierstein) finds them a storybook -- and affordable, to boot -- townhouse in Brooklyn. However, in addition to its four working fireplaces, the too-good-to-be-true offer comes with one huge, nonnegotiable glitch -- Mrs. Connelly (Eileen Essel), a wizened Irish widow quickly approaching the century mark, who lives in the rent-controlled apartment on the duplex's upper floor.

But Alex and Nancy's brownstone bliss is short-lived, as the seemingly frail pint-sized Mrs. Connelly quickly becomes a gargantuan thorn in their otherwise rosy future, souring what appeared to be a sweet steal-of-a-deal.

What starts off as a trickle of good-neighborly errands soon swells into an avalanche of around-the-clock interruptions, as the grating Gaelic granny lassoes her young landlords into full-time indentured servitude, running them ragged as they attend to her every need. Unable to deliver his manuscript on schedule because of the constant disruptions, Alex is dropped by his publisher for breach of contract. Adding to their woes, Nancy is also axed from her well-paying job.

Hard pressed to find a way out of the contractual cul-de-sac, Alex and Nancy's thoughts turn homicidal, with eviction giving way to murder as the solution of choice.

Stiller and Barrymore are pitch-perfect as the desperate young couple, leavening the film's grisly thematic undercurrents with a sympathetic likability and a good-natured willingness to suffer the brunt of the film's at-times crude sight gags and slapstick silliness in order to elicit yuks, playing honey-glazed wholesomeness and calculated cold-heartedness with equal vigor. Essel also proves brilliantly bipolar, imbuing Mrs. Connelly with an amusing blend of geriatric brittleness and crusty belligerence.

Disturbingly, much of the comedy is fueled by an ugly humor that makes light of acts which, removed from their zany, over-the-top context, are nothing to laugh at. And though the screwball premise makes for some genuinely funny moments, it is difficult -- or at least uncomfortable -- for Christians to find levity in a joke whose punch line involves murder.

Due to a black-comedy murder plot, an implied sexual encounter, recurring vulgar humor and sporadic crude language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
